lesson.grammar_point: present perfect with for and since for unfinished time (how long have you, for plus a period, since plus a starting point)

vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: a person who lives in a place
to continue to exist after something difficult or dangerous
to repair an old building so it looks the way it did before
a period of one hundred years
what is left of a very old building after most of it has fallen down
to continue to exist or to work for a long time
all the people in a family born at about the same time

paras: Most old palaces are museums. You buy a ticket, you look, and you leave. Diocletian's Palace in Split is different. The Roman emperor Diocletian built it around the year 300, as a home for his retirement, and he lived there for only a few years. But people have lived inside its walls since the seventh century, when families from a nearby Roman town ran away from a war and found safety behind the stone. So the palace has been a home for more than thirteen centuries.

Today about three thousand residents still live there. Marko, a retired teacher, has lived in a small apartment near the Peristyle, the old Roman square, since 1968. "My family has been here for four generations," he says. "My grandmother sold vegetables in this street. I have known my neighbors for fifty years." Over the decades he has seen cafes open in old Roman rooms, and he has watched the tourists arrive, more every summer.

Not everything has survived. Some parts are ruins, and people have restored some walls many times. The emperor's tomb has been a church since the seventh century, and the whole palace has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979. But for Marko, the reason it has lasted is simple. "A building survives when people use it," he says. "Museums keep stones. Families keep places alive."

listenings.text: My grandfather opened this cafe in Ljubljana in 1952, so it has been in our family for more than seventy years. I have worked here since I was sixteen. That is thirty-four years now. The tables are the same, and the old coffee machine has survived three generations of my family. Some customers have come here every morning for decades. Mr. Novak, for example, has had the same table by the window since 1980. Tourists sometimes ask me: Why don't you change anything? My answer is simple. People don't come here for new things. They come because some things last.

I have supported Hajduk Split since I was six years old. My father took me to my first game in 1961, at the old stadium in the city. Since 1979 the team has played at Poljud, by the sea, and I have had the same seat there for more than forty years. I have seen good decades and bad decades. We haven't won the league for a long time, and my wife says I am crazy. Maybe she is right. But I have never missed a derby against Dinamo since 1985. Some things a man does not stop, not even at seventy-one.

extra_audio.text: In 1968 Marko moved into a small apartment near the Peristyle. Then, for many years, he taught at a school in Split and walked home through the Roman streets. After that, in 1979, the palace became a UNESCO World Heritage Site. At that point tourists started to arrive, more every summer. Today he has lived there for more than fifty years, and he still knows every neighbor.
